steps.sub: What do you think gives the fakes away?

options.label: How they behave with the team

steps.title: Faking it
steps.html:
A television programme sends people with no experience into a job for four weeks, then asks a panel of professionals to spot them. What separates the ones who survive from the ones who don’t is rarely what you would expect.

A  The idea behind the programme is simple and slightly cruel. Producers take somebody with no experience in a particular job — a chef, a chauffeur, a fitness instructor — and give them four weeks with an expert. At the end, they must take part in a contest against real professionals, and a panel of judges has to decide which one is faking it. If the judges cannot tell, the newcomer wins.

B  Ed worked in a burger van before the programme found him. He had to be reliable and turn up for work on time; he had to be reasonably pleasant to customers; and that, more or less, was the job. He did not have to take much responsibility, because his boss dealt with the money. Four weeks later he was expected to run a professional kitchen. “Nobody tells you,” he said afterwards, “that in a real kitchen you must work to very precise times. Thirty seconds is a long time.”

C  This is where most candidates struggle, and it is not usually the technical skill that defeats them. You can teach somebody to crack an egg, flip it and get it onto a plate. You cannot teach them, in four weeks, to multitask under pressure while five other people are shouting. A chef must plan several dishes at once, hold the whole schedule in their head, and think ahead constantly. Candidates who set goals for each shift tend to survive; those who simply react do not.

D  The social rules are just as hard. Ed was shocked to realise that he could not say please and thank you all the time if he wanted the team to respect him — in a busy kitchen, a short instruction is not rudeness, it is efficiency. In other jobs the opposite applies. A chauffeur may not start a conversation with a passenger unless the passenger starts it first, and is not allowed to comment on anything they overhear. Every workplace has rules like these, and none of them are written down anywhere.

E  Judges say the giveaway is almost never a technical mistake. It is confidence in the wrong place: the candidate who explains too much, apologises too often, or checks the time. One judge put it bluntly. “A professional does not have to think about how they look. That is the difference, and you can see it in about ninety seconds.”

F  Perhaps the most useful thing the programme reveals is what a job actually consists of. We describe work in terms of qualifications and technique, but for four weeks these candidates discover something else: that most of a job is behaviour. You have to know when to speak, when to be quiet, what you are allowed to touch, and what nobody will ever explain to you. Some of them go back to their old lives afterwards. A surprising number do not.

Written for this course. The format described is based on documented reality-television ‘job swap’ programmes broadcast in the UK and elsewhere.
